entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thiemo (c. 1040, Bavaria – 1101, Jerusalem), Archbishop of Salzburg from 1090 until his death, emerged as a prominent figure in the tumultuous Investiture Controversy, a pivotal struggle between papal and imperial power that reshaped the political and religious landscape of Medieval Europe. His staunch adherence to the Gregorian Reform principles, advocating for clerical celibacy and papal supremacy over secular appointments of bishops, positioned him as a direct antagonist to Emperor Henry IV and a staunch defender of the papacy. Thiemo's trajectory from a Benedictine monk at St. Peter's Abbey, Salzburg, and later abbot of St. Peter's and St. Erentrud, reflects the era's deep entanglement of monasticism with broader ecclesiastical reform movements.

Elected Archbishop of Salzburg in 1090, Thiemo inherited a see deeply embroiled in the imperial-papal schism. His predecessor, Gebhard, had been a strong supporter of Pope Gregory VII, and Thiemo continued this legacy, refusing to be consecrated by imperial anti-bishops. This defiance led to his arrest and imprisonment by Emperor Henry IV in 1097, a stark demonstration of the Emperor's efforts to control episcopal appointments. Following his release, Thiemo embarked on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, a journey that underscored both the spiritual fervor of the age and the perilous nature of travel beyond Christendom's frontiers, culminating in his martyrdom in Jerusalem in 1101 at the hands of Saracens, though details surrounding his death remain debated.
